chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Mansur ibn Hazim from Bakr ibn Habib, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the Tashahhud, and he said: 'If it were obligatory upon people as they say, they would have perished. The people used to say the easiest thing they knew: when you praise Allah, it suffices you.'

Thus, it is not precluded that the two testimonies are obligatory, but rather it indicates that what is added to them is not obligatory, because the addition to the two testimonies is also called Tashahhud, and that which clarifies what we mentioned is [this reasoning].

key_terms.التَّشَهُّد: Tashahhud, the act of bearing witness, specifically referring to the recitation of testimonies and praise in prayer
key_terms.الشَّهَادَتَانِ: The two testimonies (La ilaha illallah, Muhammadur Rasulullah)

ai.seo_question: Is the Tashahhud in prayer obligatory or recommended in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the detailed Tashahhud is not strictly obligatory (wajib) because rigid adherence to a fixed text would burden the people, leading to potential error or omission. He establishes that while the two testimonies of faith are mandatory, the additional supplications are recommended (sunnah), reflecting the early Muslim practice of reciting whatever was easiest to remember after praising Allah. This distinction underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle of balancing ritual precision with practical ease (yusr) in acts of worship.
